record.paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
record.original_question: How much do galaxy-formation predictions change when semi-analytic models use merger trees generated by the classical extended Press-Schechter (EPS) formalism instead of merger trees extracted directly from numerical simulations, given that recent work indicates EPS may not adequately describe simulated merger trees?

evidence.quote: It is important to note that some recent work has demonstrated that this formalism might not provide an adequate description of the merger trees extracted directly from numerical simulations [8, 9, 10].

Although some of these studies have provided ‘corrections’ to analytic merger trees, many applications are still carried out using the classical EPS formalism, and little work has been done so far to understand to which measure this can affect predictions of galaxy formation models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, the assembly histories of dark-matter haloes (their "merger trees") can be generated in two distinct ways:

(1) Analytically, via the classical extended Press–Schechter (EPS) formalism, which uses the statistics of Gaussian random density fluctuations smoothed on different mass scales together with the spherical-collapse threshold to derive conditional mass functions and Monte-Carlo merger histories.

(2) Numerically, by identifying dark-matter haloes and their progenitors directly in cosmological N-body simulations and linking them across output snapshots.

Couple a fixed semi-analytic prescription for baryonic physics (gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, galaxy mergers, etc.) to merger trees obtained by each of the two methods above. Quantify how the resulting predictions of galaxy-population observables — such as the galaxy stellar mass function, the luminosity function, the cosmic star-formation history, the colour and morphology distributions, and clustering statistics — differ when EPS-based merger trees are used in place of merger trees extracted from N-body simulations. In particular, given that the EPS formalism is known to misrepresent simulated merger trees in the number of progenitors, in the growth of the main progenitor, and in the total progenitor mass, determine the magnitude and observational significance of the induced changes in galaxy-formation predictions.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent studies have addressed the comparison directly. Work coupling semi-analytic models to N-body merger trees (e.g., Helly et al. 2003; Parkinson, Cole & Helly 2008) showed that, apart from mass-resolution effects, the principal differences between EPS- and N-body-based predictions stem from known EPS deficiencies in progenitor counts, main-progenitor growth, and total progenitor mass. Modified Monte-Carlo schemes calibrated against simulations have been developed, and more recent generative/ML emulators (e.g., FLORAH-Tree, 2025) further reduce the gap. The qualitative impact on galaxy-formation predictions is now reasonably well characterized, though no fully definitive, comprehensive quantitative answer across all observables exists, so the problem is partially resolved rather than fully closed.

status_evidence.title: Constructing merger trees that mimic N-body simulations (Parkinson, Cole & Helly 2008)
status_evidence.snippet: EPS trees show non-negligible deviations from N-body trees in number of progenitors, growth of the main progenitor, and total progenitor mass; a modified Monte-Carlo scheme is calibrated to simulations.
status_evidence.claim: Quantitative discrepancies between EPS and N-body merger trees have been characterized and partially corrected.

status_evidence.title: Galaxy formation using halo merger histories taken from N-body simulations (Helly et al. 2003)
status_evidence.snippet: Couples a semi-analytic galaxy formation model to N-body merger trees and compares with EPS-based predictions.
status_evidence.claim: Direct comparison of galaxy-formation predictions using EPS vs N-body merger trees has been carried out.

status_evidence.title: FLORAH-Tree: Emulating Dark Matter Halo Merger Trees with Graph Generative Models
status_evidence.snippet: Machine-learning emulators reproduce N-body merger-rate statistics across mass and redshift, outperforming EPS.
status_evidence.claim: Recent emulators continue to refine the EPS-vs-simulation comparison, indicating ongoing development.
